title: N-Queens
statement: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal). Return all distinct solutions.
realWorld: The canonical constraint-satisfaction problem. The same search-and-prune structure underlies exam timetabling, shift rostering, frequency assignment and register allocation in compilers.

examples.explanation: A single queen on a 1x1 board.

bruteForce.idea: Generate every way to place n queens one per row and one per column — every permutation of column assignments — and test each complete arrangement for diagonal conflicts only at the end, instead of checking as each queen is placed.

complexity.time: O(n! * n) — every permutation of columns, each checked with an O(n^2) diagonal scan
complexity.space: O(n) recursion depth, plus O(n) per permutation being built

bruteForce.whySlow: Row and column conflicts are ruled out structurally by using a permutation, but the diagonal check still waits until an entire arrangement exists. Two queens colliding on a diagonal in rows 0 and 1 are still carried through every one of the remaining (n-2)! completions before the pairwise scan at the end throws each one out — the optimised version prunes that whole subtree the instant the second queen is placed. So the search still pays for the full n!, just narrowed from 'choose n of n^2 squares' down to 'permute the columns'.

patternIdentification: Constraint satisfaction with early failure detection. Since exactly one queen goes in each row, the search is a decision per row, and conflicts can be detected the moment a queen is placed — that is pruning, and it is where all the speed comes from.

optimized.idea: Place one queen per row. Track occupied columns and both diagonal families in boolean arrays so conflict checking is O(1). Cells on a '\' diagonal share (row - col); cells on a '/' diagonal share (row + col). Skip any conflicting column, which prunes its entire subtree.

commonMistakes: Scanning the board to check safety, which is O(n) per check instead of O(1) with the three boolean arrays.
Getting the diagonal index wrong; row - col ranges from -(n-1) to n-1, so it must be shifted by n-1 to index an array.
Forgetting to clear all three marks on the way out.
Validating only at row == n, which turns a pruned search back into brute-force enumeration.
